    <meta name="DC.Description" xml:lang="en" content="In 1972, Branko Grünbaum conjectured that any nontrivial arrangement of n > 2 pairwise intersecting pseudocircles in the plane can have at most 2n-2 digons (regions enclosed by exactly two pseudoarcs), with the bound being tight. While this conjecture has been confirmed for cylindrical arrangements of pseudocircles and more recently for geometric circles, we extend these results to any simple arrangement of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles." >

<div class="ltx_abstract" id="abstract">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
<p class="ltx_p">In 1972, Branko Grünbaum conjectured that any nontrivial arrangement of <math id="m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles in the plane can have at most
<math id="m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> digons (regions enclosed by exactly two pseudoarcs), with the bound being tight.
While this conjecture has been confirmed for
cylindrical arrangements of pseudocircles and more recently for geometric circles, we extend these results to any simple arrangement of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles.</p>
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In this paper we focus on families of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles. A <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">family of pseudocircles</em> is a set <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> of simple closed Jordan curves in the plane such that every two of them are either disjoint, meet at exactly one point in which they touch or intersect at exactly two
points in which they properly cross each other. The <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">arrangement</em> <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is the cell complex into which the plane is decomposed by the pseudocircles in <math id="S1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math>. It consists of vertices, edges and faces. The arrangement is called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">trivial</em> if there are two points that lie on every pseudocircle in <math id="S1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math>. If there is no point that lies on three pseudocircles, then both the
arrangement and <math id="S1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> are called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">simple</em>.
Note that every simple arrangement of more than two pseudocircles is nontrivial. The arrangement is called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pairwise intersecting</em> if any two pseudocircles intersect in exactly two points.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">digon</em> is a face in the arrangement that is bounded by exactly two edges. If the two edges of a digon are contained in pseudocircles <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, respectively, then we say that <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">form</em> that digon and that each of <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">supports</em> it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A trivial arrangement of <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math> pseudocircles contains <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n" display="inline"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> digons for <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>1" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. In his 1972 monograph “Arrangements and Spreads” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> Branko Grünbaum conjectured that for nontrivial arrangements of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles the maximum number of digons is <math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_conjecture">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conjecture 1</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Grünbaum’s digon conjecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, Conjecture 3.6]</cite>)<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Every nontrivial arrangement of <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles has at most <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> digons.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">This conjecture was accompanied by a construction with exactly <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> digons, see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for an example with six pseudocircles. This example can be easily extended by adding new pseudocircles to the four in the middle, which illustrates that the bound in Conjecture <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Conjecture 1 (Grünbaum’s digon conjecture [11, Conjecture 3.6]). ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is tight. With some care, this construction can even be realized with geometric circles.
A different construction appears in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2n-2.pdf2svg.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="240" height="169" style="width: 480px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A family of 6 pseudocircles forming 10 digons.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Conjecture <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Conjecture 1 (Grünbaum’s digon conjecture [11, Conjecture 3.6]). ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> was shown to be true in several special cases (assuming simple arrangements).
Agarwal et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> showed that Conjecture <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Conjecture 1 (Grünbaum’s digon conjecture [11, Conjecture 3.6]). ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is true for <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cylindrical</em> arrangements, these are arrangements for which there is a point that is surrounded by each of the pseudocircles.
More recently, Conjecture <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Conjecture 1 (Grünbaum’s digon conjecture [11, Conjecture 3.6]). ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> was studied and advertised by Felsner, Roch and Scheucher <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> who showed that it holds for arrangements in which there are three pseudocircles such that every two of them form a digon.
This new interest in Grünbaum’s conjecture has also
motivated us to study the problem. First, we were able to show in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> that Grünbaum’s conjecture is true for simple arrangements of pairwise intersecting geometric circles. Here, using ideas from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> we prove:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Every simple arrangement of <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles has at most <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> digons. This bound is tight.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Our proof is inspired by the proof technique introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> for bounding the number of digons in cylindrical arrangements of <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline"><mi>n</mi></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles.
In that paper, a bipartite graph is associated to a cylindrical arrangement in a way that each pseudocircle is represented by a single point which is its intersection with a common fixed transversal line.
The edges of this graph correspond to digons and are drawn according to a simple yet clever rule such that every two independent edges cross an even number of times. The Strong Hanani-Tutte Theorem (see below) then implies that the drawn (bipartite) graph is planar and hence by Euler’s formula has at most <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-4" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> edges.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">For the general case of Grünbaum’s conjecture, we combine a modification of this graph drawing technique and a graph <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">doubling</em> technique that was used for the case of geometric circles in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
Namely, a bipartite graph is drawn such that every pseudocircle is represented by <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">two</em> points which are its intersection with a common transversal pseudocircle.
Furthermore, every digon is represented by <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">two</em> edges that are drawn following a rule in the spirit of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> such that every two independent edges cross an even number of times.
Therefore, the drawn (bipartite) graph is planar and hence has at most <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2(2n)-4=4n-4" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> edges, representing at most <math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> digons.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Note that our result can be applied for bounding the number of <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">touching points</em> in simple arrangements where any two pseudocircles intersect or touch. In any such arrangement of <math id="S1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pseudocircles, one can turn each touching point into exactly one digon between the two pseudocircles that support the touching. Therefore, for simple arrangements, an upper bound on the number of digons translates directly to a bound on the number of touching pairs or equivalently (in this case) touching points. One can also turn each digon into exactly one touching point in the case of simple arrangements if <math id="S1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>3" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, but for <math id="S1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=3" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, two pseudocircles may touch the third one at separate points forming a single digon (the region bounded by the entire third pseudocircle), see Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In this scenario, turning the digon into a touching point would reduce the third pseudocircle to a single point, which is degenerate, and the final arrangement would violate the assumptions on the number of crossings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="n_3.pdf2svg.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="299" height="182" style="width: 598px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">If we allow touchings and <math id="S1.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=3" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, then a digon might be surrounded by only one pseudocircle.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">The transformation from digons to touching points or vice versa keeps their sum constant at every step (except for <math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> or in the above-mentioned case), therefore they are equivalent for <math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>3" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. From Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we have:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 3</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Every simple arrangement of pseudocircles where any two pseudocircles intersect or touch has at most <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> touching pairs of pseudocircles. For <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>3" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, the sum of digons and touching pairs is at most <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2n-2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Outline</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> we collect useful observations and results that we need for the main proof. In Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Proof of Theorem 2 ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> we prove Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Concluding remarks ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> we discuss some open questions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Some terminology and tools</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We begin with some simple definitions and observations, some of which also appear in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> in the context of circles.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> be a simple family of <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles in the plane. We may assume (and we will assume from now on) that every pseudocircle in <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> supports at least one digon. Otherwise, we can remove any pseudocircle from <math id="S2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> that does not satisfy this condition and argue for the remaining family of pseudocircles.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As touchings are forbidden in a pairwise intersecting family, each digon is supported by exactly two pseudocircles. A digon is called a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lens</em> if it is surrounded by both supporting pseudocircles, and it is called a <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">lune</em> otherwise. A lune must be surrounded by precisely one of its supporting pseudocircles, while lying outside the region surrounded by the other (see Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Here we ignore the case where the unbounded face is a digon.
This indeed can be avoided by means of a simple inversion of the plane.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="lens_lune.pdf2svg.svg" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="299" height="99" style="width: 598px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A lens and a lune.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A pseudocircle <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> is <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">internal</em> if it supports a digon that is surrounded by <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and it is called <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">external</em> if it supports a digon (necessarily a
lune) that is not surrounded by <math id="S2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>. The following simple observation is important for the proof.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 4</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A pseudocircle in <math id="Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> cannot be both internal and external.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Proof.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Assume to the contrary that there is a pseudocircle <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow></math> which is both external and internal. This means that there exist <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1},c_{2}\in{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow></math> such that <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> form a digon not surrounded by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> while <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> form a digon that is surrounded by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> (see Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="int_ext.pdf2svg.svg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="232" height="157" style="width: 464px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A pseudocircle cannot be both internal and external.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In such a case <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> cannot intersect, contradicting our assumption that we have an arrangement of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles. Indeed, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> cannot cross in the region surrounded by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> because that subarc of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> is an edge of a digon. Similarly, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> cannot intersect in the complementary region of the plane because that subarc of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> is an edge of an other digon.
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hfill\blacktriangleleft" display="inline"><mo>◀</mo></math></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Any simple closed Jordan curve in the plane divides the plane into two parts, one bounded (the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">interior</em>) and the other unbounded (the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">exterior</em>). We will refer to these two parts as the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regions</em> of the curve.
For a pseudocircle <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow></math>, we will call the region that contains the digons supported by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">digon-region</em> of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>. By Proposition <a href="#Thmtheorem4" title="Proposition 4. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and because we assume that every pseudocircle supports at least one digon, every pseudocircle in <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> has exactly one digon-region. One advantage of this definition is that we can treat lunes and lenses in a uniform way: every digon is just the intersection of the digon-regions of the two corresponding pseudocircles supporting it.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>Another way to think about this is to imagine that we work on a sphere, and we have caps corresponding to the digon-regions.</span></span></span> This will simplify the case-analysis in some of the proofs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">It is well-known that any family of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles can be extended to a larger family of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles, and the following lemma shows that we can also do it without destroying the existing digons.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem5" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 5</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> be a simple family of <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles. Then there is a closed curve <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> such that <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}\cup\{c\}" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is a simple family of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles, and furthermore <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> does not intersect any of the digons in <math id="Thmtheorem5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Proof.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> be a pseudocircle in <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math>. From Proposition <a href="#Thmtheorem4" title="Proposition 4. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> we know that one of the two regions of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> (the one that is not the digon-region of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>) does not contain any digon supported by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>. Let <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> be a curve that is running very close to <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> outside of the digon-region of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>. Then <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> intersects each pseudocircle in <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}\setminus\{\alpha\}" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> exactly twice and it intersects no digon of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
However, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> does not intersect <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>. In order to fix this, we notice that because <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> is a simple arrangement of pseudocircles, there is a subarc <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math> of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> that is disjoint from any digon supported by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and consequently it is disjoint from any digon in <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. We can modify <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> along <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline"><mi>s</mi></math> such that the resulting simple closed curve crosses <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> at two points yielding the desired extension of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> (see Figure <a href="#S2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hfill\blacktriangleleft" display="inline"><mo>◀</mo></math></p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="canon.pdf2svg.svg" id="S2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" width="236" height="232" style="width: 472px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Extending <math id="S2.F5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> with a curve <math id="S2.F5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> which avoids the digons in <math id="S2.F5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> and intersects every pseudocircle in <math id="S2.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> exactly twice.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">For a pseudocircle <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> with a given orientation as a closed curve and points <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{1},v_{2}" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> on <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> we denote by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[v_{1},v_{2}]_{\alpha}" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>α</mi></msub></math> (resp., <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v_{1},v_{2})_{\alpha}" display="inline"><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>α</mi></msub></math>) the closed (resp., open) segment of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> from <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> to <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> following <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> in the given orientation.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem6" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_prop">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 6</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},c\}" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> be a simple family of pairwise intersecting pseudocircles
such that <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> form a digon.
Suppose that <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> is oriented and let <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{j}^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>in</mi></msubsup></math> (resp., <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{j}^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>out</mi></msubsup></math>) be the intersection point of <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{j}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> in which <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> enters (resp., leaves) the digon-region of <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{j}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, for <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=1,2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></math>.
Then <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}^{\rm in},\alpha_{1}^{\rm out},\alpha_{2}^{\rm in},\alpha_{2}^{\rm
out}" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> is the cyclic order along <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> of the four intersection points of <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> with <math id="Thmtheorem6.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3" class="ltx_subparagraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subparagraph">Proof.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">If <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}^{\rm in}\in(\alpha_{1}^{\rm in},\alpha_{1}^{\rm out})_{c}" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> or <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}^{\rm out}\in(\alpha_{1}^{\rm in},\alpha_{1}^{\rm out})_{c}" display="inline"><mrow><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math>, then we have a point from <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}\cap c" display="inline"><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∩</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> which lies in the digon-region of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>.
However, the intersection of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> with the digon-region of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> consists only of the subarc of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> which bounds the digon formed by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}" display="inline"><msub><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>.
This implies that <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> intersects this digon which is impossible.
Therefore, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup></math> must follow <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{1}^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup></math> in the cyclic order and, similarly, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>out</mi></msubsup></math> must follow <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{2}^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msubsup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>in</mi></msubsup></math>.
<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hfill\blacktriangleleft" display="inline"><mo>◀</mo></math></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.P0.SPx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">A <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">topological graph</em> is a graph drawn in the plane such that its vertices are drawn as distinct points and its edges are drawn as Jordan arcs connecting the corresponding points.
Apart from its endpoints, an edge of a topological graph cannot contain any drawn vertex.
Furthermore, every two edges in a topological graph intersect at a finite number of points, each of which is either a common endpoint or a crossing point.
A graph is <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">planar</em> if it can be drawn as a topological graph where no pair of edges crosses.
By the Strong Hanani-Tutte Theorem, it is enough to require an even number of crossings between independent edges.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>Two edges are <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">independent</em> if they do not share an endpoint.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem7" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 7</span></span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Strong Hanani-Tutte Theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>)<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span>
</h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p"><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A graph is planar if and only if it can be drawn as a topological graph in which every two independent edges cross an even number of times.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Proof of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>
</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">As we noted in the beginning of Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we can suppose that <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> is a simple family of <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n>2" display="inline"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> pairwise intersecting pseudocircles in the plane such that every pseudocircle in <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> supports at least one digon.
By Lemma <a href="#Thmtheorem5" title="Lemma 5. ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> there is a simple closed curve <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> that intersects each pseudocircle in <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> twice but does not intersect the digons of the arrangement <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. We fix the counterclockwise orientation on <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>. Whenever we traverse <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> or consider a cyclic order of points on it, we do it according to this orientation. Recall that <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> is an auxiliary pseudocircle and it is not a member of <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math>; in particular we do not care about digons supported by <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Every pseudocircle <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow></math> intersects <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> at two points such that at one of them <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> enters the digon-region of <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and at the other <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> leaves this digon-region. We denote these points by <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math>, respectively. See for example Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3 Proof of Theorem 2 ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. In this figure, the digon-regions of <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> are the interior regions of these curves, whereas the digon-region of <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math> is its exterior region.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="G.pdf2svg.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="354" height="250" style="width: 708px; height: unset; max-width: 100%"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Three pseudocircles <math id="S3.F6.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>, <math id="S3.F6.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math> and <math id="S3.F6.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> and a drawing of the corresponding bipartite double cover graph <math id="S3.F6.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>. For example, <math id="S3.F6.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and <math id="S3.F6.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> form a digon, hence we draw the edges <math id="S3.F6.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\gamma^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.F6.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\alpha^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> along <math id="S3.F6.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>. Considering the (blue) edge <math id="S3.F6.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\alpha^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, starting at <math id="S3.F6.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> (resp., <math id="S3.F6.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math>) and following <math id="S3.F6.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math> towards the interior of <math id="S3.F6.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>, we first encounter <math id="S3.F6.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> (resp., <math id="S3.F6.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math>). Therefore, the drawn edge <math id="S3.F6.m37" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\alpha^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> “passes by” <math id="S3.F6.m38" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> (resp., <math id="S3.F6.m39" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math>) within the exterior (resp., interior) of <math id="S3.F6.m40" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>. Each pseudocircle’s label is placed within the digon-region associated with that pseudocircle.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>The digon graph and its double cover</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">In order to bound from above the number of digons in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> we consider the graph <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> whose
vertex set corresponds to the pseudocircles in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> and whose edge set corresponds to pairs of pseudocircles which form a digon in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>
(since <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is nontrivial and intersecting a pair of pseudocircles may not form more than one digon).
We call <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">digon graph</em> of the arrangement.
Bounding the number of edges in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> is equivalent to bounding the number of digons in <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">For our proof, we consider the <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bipartite double cover</em> of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math> - this graph, denote it by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>, has two vertices, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> for every vertex <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>, and two edges, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta^{\rm out},\alpha^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for every edge <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha,\beta)" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{d}" display="inline"><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></math>.
Thus, the number of edges of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> is twice the number of digons in <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>.
By construction <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> is bipartite.
It remains to show that <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> is also planar and therefore has at most <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2|V(G)|-4=4n-4" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>⁢</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow></math> edges. This will prove Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Drawing <math id="S3.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>𝑮</mi></math> in the plane</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We draw <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> as a topological graph in the plane.
By abuse of notation, we will not distinguish between <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> and its drawing.
The vertices of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> are represented by the points <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\alpha^{\rm in}\mid\alpha\in{\cal{F}}\}\cup\{\alpha^{\rm out}\mid\alpha\in{%
\cal{F}}\}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></math> as defined above.
Thus, for every two pseudocircles <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha,\beta\in{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow></math> that form a digon in <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{A}}({\cal{F}})" display="inline"><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> there should be two drawn edges <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta^{\rm out},\alpha^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.
These edges will satisfy the following properties:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">An edge <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> connects <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> and <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math>, while avoiding all other vertices of <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>;</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">every two edges intersect finitely many times; and</p>
</div>
</li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iii)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">an edge <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> follows very closely the subarc of <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> starting at <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> and ending at <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math>, counterclockwise along <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>. It may cross the curve <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> several times, but it does not intersect the digon-regions of neither <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> nor <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Properties (i), (ii), and (iii) can be easily satisfied.
For the second part of (iii) note that Proposition <a href="#Thmtheorem6" title="Proposition 6. ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> implies that when following <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> from <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> we remain outside the digon-regions of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We need one more property that the drawing of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
should satisfy. This is the most crucial property for the proof and it has to do with
how <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is drawn with respect to the intermediate
vertices of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> along the arc on <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> from <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math>. We use a modification of the drawing rule that appears in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in V" display="inline"><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> be an intermediate vertex of <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> on <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> along the arc from <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math>
to <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math>. We will need to indicate whether the edge <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
passes near <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> in the interior region of <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> or in its exterior region.
In the first case, we say that the edge <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">passes <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> from the inside</em> whereas in the second case it <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">passes <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> from the outside</em>. Other than these inside/outside decisions and properties (i)-(iii), <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be drawn arbitrarily.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We determine whether <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> passes <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> from the inside or
from the outside according to the value <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> that we define in the following way.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> be the pseudocircle in <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> that intersects <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math> at <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math>. It follows from Proposition <a href="#Thmtheorem6" title="Proposition 6. ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> that <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> must be different from <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math>. We follow the curve <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math> starting from <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> in the direction <em class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">entering the interior region of <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math></em>.
If we intersect <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math> sooner than we intersect <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math>, then <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))=1" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, otherwise <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))=2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>Thus, the value <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline"><mn>1</mn></math> or <math id="footnote3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline"><mn>2</mn></math> represents whether we encounter the first or the second pseudocircle among the two pseudocircles of the ordered pair <math id="footnote3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.</span></span></span> Since <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal{F}}" display="inline"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></math> is a simple family of pairwise intersecting curves, <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> is well-defined.
If <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))=1" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, then we pass <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> from the inside. Otherwise <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(v,(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in}))=2" display="inline"><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁢</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and we pass <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline"><mi>v</mi></math> from the outside.
See Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3 Proof of Theorem 2 ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Having described the drawing of the graph <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> in the plane, we will conclude the proof by showing that every two independent edges of <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> cross an even number of times which implies that <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math> is planar by the Strong Hanani-Tutte Theorem (Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem7" title="Theorem 7 (Strong Hanani-Tutte Theorem [20]). ‣ Proof. ‣ 2 Some terminology and tools ‣ The Maximum Number of Digons Formed by Pairwise Intersecting Pseudocircles" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">
<span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Independent edges cross evenly</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\delta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be two independent edges of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline"><mi>G</mi></math>.
The parity of the number of crossings between two edges depends solely on how one edge passes by a vertex of the other edge.
For example, if the cyclic order of their endpoints is <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha^{\rm out},\gamma^{\rm out},\delta^{\rm in},\beta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></mrow></math>, then the two edges cross evenly if and only if <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> passes by both of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma^{\rm out}" display="inline"><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta^{\rm in}" display="inline"><msup><mi>δ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup></math> from the inside or both of them from the outside.
Therefore, it is enough to consider all the possible topologically different arrangements of the at most four involved pseudocircles (actually five because of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline"><mi>c</mi></math>) and verify that in each of them <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\delta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> cross an even number of times.
Using a computer we have verified this, still, for the remainder of the section (and of the proof) we provide a non-computer-aided proof.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p class="ltx_p">We begin by observing that it is enough to consider the case that the involved pseudocircles <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline"><mi>α</mi></math>, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline"><mi>β</mi></math>, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline"><mi>γ</mi></math>, and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline"><mi>δ</mi></math> are distinct.
Indeed, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha^{\rm out},\beta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>α</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma^{\rm out},\delta^{\rm in})" display="inline"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>out</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>δ</mi><mi>in</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are independent edges, therefore, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\neq\gamma" display="inline"><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\neq\delta" display="inline"><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></math>.
